blocks.html: 🎼 Universal Requirements.
For the sake of simplicity, the terms of 'Resume' and 'CV' are to be considered interchangeable.
Although formatting and content recommendations will vary from situation to situation, some elements should feature on all CVs.
Contact Essentials.
Your first and last name (and your preferred pronouns, if you so desire).
Your e-mail address, which should be rendered as highlightable text.
Your phone number, ideally including international calling code.
Your portfolio or website URL, which should be both highlightable, as well as, ideally, a clickable link.

Note that if you host your CV in a publicly-accessible space, such as on your website, you should consider publishing a bespoke version that does not include your phone number and/or e-mail as to avoid unscrupulous individuals, or bots from scraping your document to harvest your personal information.
Length & Layout Guidelines.
Things have changed a lot since we have almost entirely moved from the paper to digital age, and some of the rules that might have once applied are no longer as important.

The most common example is the widespread obsession in having a CV fit on a single page. What is far more important than the number of pages is an effective layout with a strong hierarchy, allowing easy digestion of the content on the page(s). Furthermore, in an industry where it is not uncommon to change studio every couple years, for many people, keeping all of their experience on a single page simply won't be possible without making major concessions in more important areas of presentation.

As with everything though, moderation is key, and whilst you shouldn't worry about having a 2-page CV, if you find yourself reaching 3 pages or above, it might be worth reconsidering your formatting and/or content.

Another formatting aspect to keep in mind, is that if you feel it would benefit your presentation, there is no reason to prevent yourself from deviating from the standard 'Portrait' orientation, and moving towards a 'Landscape' orientation more suited for desktop consumption.

Unlike the ‣, it is not absolutely essential for you to create bespoke CVs for each employer. However, in special circumstances, it can be to your benefit to further customise your CV to better represent your relevance to the role and/or company.
Displaying Your Portrait.
A very common question from job-seekers revolves around the hesitation in including a photograph of themselves as part of their CV.

The general consenus on this is that including a photograph of yourself is disrecommended as it may introduce unwanted biases into the review process. There have even been Diversity & Inclusion initiatives in certain workplaces that have gone as far as to remove candidate names prior to application reviews in order to reduce these effects (this is not something you have to worry about or action on your end though).
With that said, it is entirely your choice if you wish to include your photograph. It really comes whether you think there is a higher chance that it will benefit, or penalise you.

For example, one argument in favour of including a great, professionally-taken photograph is that it can help in further injecting perceptions of professionalism, personal brand, and/or potentially even authority, into the persona you are putting foward.
Using Skills Graphs.
Bluntly put, skills graphs are a running joke amongst hiring managers, and you should not include these in your CV.

Any perceived aesthetic quality gained by the inclusion of skill-related infographics will immediately be outweighed by any one of the reasons why they are a terrible idea, and are ultimately, completely meaningless as a piece of information.
🖋️ Special Requirements for Designers.
One area where Designers are expected to go above and beyond with their CVs compared to much of the general population, is excellence in presentation.
The Importance of Graphic Design.

As someone proclaiming themselves an expert in a visual design field, it is essential that your CV completely reflects this. Often serving as a very first impression, the presentation of your CV must be an example of your very best design sensibilities, and almost serve as a 'portfolio piece' in itself, and a model of your ability to balance functionality and style.

With that said, standard text-editors such as Word, or Google Docs, simply will not cut it, and you should instead be crafting your CV in purpose-built publishing software such as Adobe InDesign, Affinity Publisher, or even Adobe Illustrator which will give you the tools you need to not only produce high-precision work, but also allow you far greater stylistic expression.
File Format Expectations.

Unlike other disciplines, who might be able to get away with using .doc files, you will need to not only ensure that your CV is a perfect reproduction of your designs regardless of the machine it is viewed on, but will also need to ensure that text remains fully-selectable (and interactive).
Because of these two requirements, the .pdf format will be your best bet.

Although some candidates worry about .pdf-formatted files not being recognised by automated CV-processing software used by studios, almost all online application portals will clearly state which document types are accepted, and you will be very hard-pressed to find any companies in the industry who do not include the .pdf as one of them.

One other constraint that application portals will often include is a limit on file size. It is always worth performing some compression tests to see how small you can get your document before starting to lose image quality. The smaller you can get, the better, as you will run into far less issues when uploading to various websites.
☠️ CV Content Skeleton.
Although you can sculpt the body of your CV with a fair amount of freedom, there are certain essential elements that should be represented in almost all cases.
Work Experience.
This should by far represent the majority of your content, and should have a place of prominence within your layout.
The following should be included at minimum for each workplace you have served at:
Company Name, and Location.

Official title(s) held, and date range during which the title(s) were held.
If you changed titles within a company, it can be incredibly beneficial to list each one (and their dates) as a separate line item. It's a really effective, tangible way to showcase a studio recognising your increasing growth and rise in value within the organisation.

Games developed whilst at a studio.
It can also be helpful to state which platforms each title was developed for, as a show of technical experience.
If you have worked with development partners, or publishers, you can also mention this in a format along the lines of "Big Game (PC), in partnership with Big Game Corp."
If any titles are either cancelled, or not yet released, it is perfectly acceptable to list a title as "Unreleased Title", or if some information is available to the public, even going as far as something along the lines of "Unannounced PC Shooter". Just make sure you don't make the mistake of revealing anything under NDA. It's not uncommon for the press to scour LinkedIn or resumes to look for these kind of errors, to then publicise. This could land you in hot water.
Responsibilites and/or Areas of Focus.
What to do in the event of having no previous studio experience.
Educational Experience.

Note that although formal educational background matters far less than your Portfolio, it is still a good idea to include any post-secondary education you have completed, as either further proof of training in your specialty, or even as a great conversation-starter if you have studied something completely different.
Where you went to school, during what time frame, and the location of the institution.
What you studied, and any accolades received.
Skills.
The skills section is a great place to list out:
Any software packages you have experience with.
Any languages you speak.
Any programming languages you are proficient in.
Any technology you have experience in, such as game engines, or UI middleware solutions.
A list of platforms you have developed for (especially if not included as part of your work experience).
Any soft-skills you feel particularly competent in.
Personal Brief.

Somewhere on your CV, you should include a small blurb about who you are, with an expression of your mission statement. This should feel in a lot of ways like a one-to-two sentence Cover Letter, so don't hesitate to customise it for each position you apply to.
Nice-to-Haves.
Although these are not essential, they can add a lot to your CV:
Any volunteer work you have performed, even if completley unrelated to work.
Any public speaking experience, or any publications you have authored.

A list of personal interests and/or a list of some of your favourite games.
Although listing your favourite games would be seen as completely irrelevant in other industries, it is almost guaranteed that the person reviewing, and subsequently interviewing you, plays video games. With that said, it can serve as both an excellent ice-breaker, and a way to showcase your interest in products similar to those you will potentially be working on.
Do Not Include.
Age, or Date-of-Birth.
Anything else that your potential future employer has absolutely no business knowing about you, as listed in the Forbidden Questions.

It goes without saying that you should never, ever lie or inflate facts or responsilities on your CV.
The industry is incredibly small and it is likely that any attempts at deception will not only prevent you from accessing the role you are applying to, but likely many others for years to come due to acquiring a reputation as a fraud.
